24.text: In 1897, when engaged in preparing a census of the Chukchee in the

25.text: Kolyma district, I had occasion to ascertain that about one-third of all the

26.text: women had had one or several divorces. Of the children born during these

27.text: marriages, some were living in the husbands’ families, and some in those of

28.text: the wives. Such children, left without a proper home, are regarded as

29.text: belonging to the entire family, and are much cared for by all its members.

30.text: The same applies to natural children borne by unmarried women.

31.text: Polygyny. — The majority of the Chukchee are monogamists; in some

32.text: localities, however, one-third and more, of all the marriages, are polygynous.

33.text: The Reindeer Chukchee generally ascribe polygyny to economic consid-

34.text: erations. “If I possess one herd, I need but one house and one wife to look

35.text: after it; if, however, I own two herds, I must have two separate households

36.text: and a woman for each of them.” There is some truth in this assertion.

41.text: M. Turner (Hudson Bay Eskimo, p. 189) says of the Hudson Bay Eskimo, “A man seldom keeps a wife for

42.text: a number of years.... In rare instances, where there is compatibility of temper, the pair remain together

43.text: for life.” In the same way the Chukchee marriage is easily dissolved in its first period, but grows in force

44.text: with the course of time. Franz Boas (Central Eskimo, p. 579) mentions also that among the Central Eskimo
